newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Currency boards need good financial system - BIS.
newsitem.headline: Currency boards need good financial system - BIS.

text.p: Currency boards, a system Bulgaria will adopt on July 1, offer several advantages, but countries can face problems managing fragile financial systems when there is no lender of last resort, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said.

Faced with a rapid withdrawal of bank deposits, a collapse of the exchange rate, soaring inflation and plummeting growth, Bulgaria will join the other transition economies of Estonia and Lithuania in adopting a currency board system.

Currency board systems have been instrumental in bringing down inflation and building credibility, for example in Argentina, which adopted a currency-board-like system in 1991, BIS said in its 67th annual report.

BIS also said that currency boards were useful for immature financial markets or institutions with limited policy-making experience and reduces the scope for outside political pressure by tying the hands of the monetary authorities.
However, currency boards are subject to three sources of vulnerability, which -- as in the case of Lithuania -- may force a loosening of the rules.
Firstly, the real exchange rate could become misaligned and a drop in inflation is not instantaneous so there is some erosion of competitiveness in the initial stages of a currency board.
Secondly, their credibility depends to a large extent on fiscal policy and only when financing requirements are modest will pressures for central bank credit be absent.
Thirdly, it can be problematic managing a fragile financial system in the absence of a lender of last resort, BIS said.

It noted that Argentina, Estonia and Lithuania had to deal with banking sector problems and Argentina was able to deal with the sharp reduction in domestic liquidity triggered by the Mexican crisis in early 1995.
Estonia, however, appeared to have had less flexibility and allowed a large bank to fail in 1992, at great cost to depositors and shareholders.
"This puts a premium on ensuring that the major building-blocks of a robust financial system are in place," BIS said.

The principles of a currency board include a rigid exchange rate link to a reserve currency, the issue of base money only in exchange for the equivalent amount of foreign exchange and no central bank lending.
